Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat al-Waqi'ah (the Inevitable Event)

It is a Meccan surah. It is related from Masruq that he said: "Whoever wishes to know the news of the first and the last, the news of the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire, and the news of this world and the Hereafter, let him recite Surat al-Waqi'ah." And Allah knows best.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When the Inevitable Event occurs﴾. Its meaning: when the Resurrection comes to be, and this is the view of the majority of the exegetes (mufassirun). The Resurrection was named "al-Waqi'ah" (the Event that occurs) because its occurrence is inevitable. The Arabs call everything expected that must happen "waqi'" (occurring). Al-Dahhak said: "Al-Waqi'ah here is the Blast (al-Sayhah) that causes the death of all creatures." It was also said: the Resurrection was named al-Waqi'ah because of the great severity that befalls in it. And it is related from some of them: because it occurs upon people while they are heedless.

If it is asked: where is the answer (jawab) to His saying ﴿idha﴾ (when)? This word must have an answer, and the answer is: its answer is His saying ﴿then those on the right hand﴾.

And His saying: ﴿There will be no denying of its occurrence﴾. Qatadah said: "It is not a repetition, nor a reversal, nor a return." It is also said that its meaning is: it is true, and there is no falsehood in it. It was also said: "It means there is no soul that lies about its occurrence," related from Sufyan. Its meaning is: at the time of its occurrence, there will be no one who denies it.

The commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on Surah 56, verse 3:

And His saying: ﴿Abasing [some], exalting [others]﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it abases some peoples and exalts others. And from him, in another narration: it abases peoples who were exalted, and exalts peoples who were abased in the world. And on the authority of al-Suddi: it exalts some peoples in Paradise and abases some peoples in the Fire. The meaning of this is: it abases the people of disobedience by making the Fire necessary for them, and exalts the people of obedience by making Paradise necessary for them. Ibn Jurayj said: ﴿abasing, exalting﴾ by good deeds and bad deeds.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 4:

The words of the Most High: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾. Al-Mubarrad said: "The rajja (violent shaking) is a movement from which a sound is heard, and it is more intense than the sayha (cry/blast). Based on this, the meaning of the verse is: the earth was set in motion together with those upon it." This is in the same sense as the words of the Most High: ﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) earthquake﴾.

And His saying: ﴿And the mountains will be crumbled to dust﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: they will be crushed into fine powder. It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri: they will be uprooted from their base. As-Suddi said: they will be broken into pieces. Mujahid said: they will be made to crumble like sawiq (roasted-grain flour) is crumbled, that is, they will be ground fine; al-bisisah is the fine flour, and sawiq is moistened and made into provisions. Qatadah said: "they will be crumbled" means they will become like a crumbling tree that the winds scatter. The poet also used bass in the sense of mixing (later translated as "moisten"):

(Do not knead [it] kneading, nor crumble [it] crumbling...)

It was cited by an-Nahhas. Some of them said: "bussat" means "sayyarat" (they will be set in motion), and from this is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "A people will come out from Madinah, and Madinah is better for them," meaning they will travel.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 6:

And His saying: ﴿And they shall become scattered dust specks.﴾ ʿAlī (may Allah be pleased with him) said: It is what rises from the hooves of horses, from the pounded ground and the dust, and then vanishes.

And it is related from some of them: The scattered dust (al-habāʾ al-munbath) is that which is seen in a window from the light of the sun, like a stretched-out pillar.

The more correct view is the first: it is the scattered dust (al-habāʾ al-munbath). And it is related from some of them: that the scattered dust is ash.
"And His saying: ﴿And you were three kinds﴾ — i.e., three categories."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verses 8–9:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand? And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ Yazid ibn Aslam said: They are those who were taken from the right side of Adam, peace be upon him, and the companions of the left hand are those who were taken from the left side. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: The companions of the right hand are those who are given their book in their right hands, and the companions of the left hand are those who are given their book in their left hands. As-Suddi said: The companions of the right hand are the majority of the people of Paradise, and the companions of the left hand are the majority of the people of Hell. It is also said: The companions of the right hand are those who are blessed (mayamin) in regard to their own souls, and the companions of the left hand are those who are ill-omened (mashi'im) in regard to their own souls. The Arabs call the left side al-janib al-ash'am, they call the left hand ash-shu'ma, and the right hand al-yumna.

And His saying: ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ and ﴿What are the companions of the left hand?﴾ This, in the speech of the Arabs, is for expressing wonder (ta'ajjub), and in the speech of Allah with His servants it is to alert (tanbih) to the great importance of the matter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verses 8–9:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿So the companions of the right hand—what are the companions of the right hand? And the companions of the left hand—what are the companions of the left hand?﴾ Yazid ibn Aslam said: They are those who were taken from the right side of Adam, peace be upon him, and the companions of the left hand are those who were taken from the left side. It is narrated from Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi that he said: The companions of the right hand are those who are given their book in their right hands, and the companions of the left hand are those who are given their book in their left hands. As-Suddi said: The companions of the right hand are the majority of the people of Paradise, and the companions of the left hand are the majority of the people of Hell. It is also said: The companions of the right hand are those who are blessed (mayamin) in regard to their own souls, and the companions of the left hand are those who are ill-omened (mashi'im) in regard to their own souls. The Arabs call the left side al-janib al-ash'am, they call the left hand ash-shu'ma, and the right hand al-yumna.

And His saying: ﴿What are the companions of the right hand?﴾ and ﴿What are the companions of the left hand?﴾ This, in the speech of the Arabs, is for expressing wonder (ta'ajjub), and in the speech of Allah with His servants it is to alert (tanbih) to the great importance of the matter.

And His saying: ﴿And the foremost, the foremost﴾. Ka'b said: they are the prophets, peace be upon them. It is also reported from some of them that they are everyone who prayed towards the two qiblas (al-qiblatayn, the two directions of prayer: Jerusalem and the Ka'bah). It is reported from Ibn 'Abbas, in some narrations, that the believer of Pharaoh's family preceded to Musa, the believer of the family of Yasin preceded to Isa, and Ali preceded to Muhammad in faith. Abu al-Husayn ibn Faris narrated it. It is also said: the foremost are those who hasten to acts of obedience.

And His saying: ﴿the foremost﴾. The sense of the verse is: and the foremost in good deeds and acts of obedience are the foremost in ranks. It has also been said that this is by way of emphasis.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 11:

And His saying: ﴿Those are the ones brought near﴾, meaning: those brought near in rank, in honour, and in arrival at the pleasure of Allah, the Exalted.

He mentions in another place three categories, saying: ﴿Then We gave the Book as an inheritance to those whom We chose from among Our servants; but among them is one who wrongs himself, and among them is one who is moderate, and among them is one who is foremost in good deeds﴾. Some of the people of tafsir (exegesis) held that the categories mentioned in Surah al-Waqi'ah are all from among the believers, like the categories mentioned in that surah, and that the companions of the left (ashab al-mash'amah) are those who wrong themselves, the companions of the right (ashab al-maymanah) are the moderate, and the foremost (al-sabiqun) are those foremost in good deeds. The first view is the more sound, that the companions of the left are the disbelievers; and because Allah, the Exalted, said after it: ﴿But the companions of the left: what of the companions of the left? In scorching wind and boiling water﴾, and He described them with disbelief, as will come.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 56, verse 12:

And His saying: ﴿In gardens of bliss﴾. Al-Naqqash mentioned in his tafsir, from the Prophet (ﷺ), in describing the Garden of Bliss: "That one brick of it is silver and one brick is gold, its clay is musk, its dust is saffron, and its pebbles are pearls and rubies."
His saying: ﴿A multitude of the earlier peoples﴾, meaning: a company (jama'ah) of the earlier peoples. The word thullah (ثلة) is derived from ath-thall (الثل), which means a cutting-off.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 14:

And His saying: ﴿And a few from the later generations﴾. The people of tafsir (exegesis) differed regarding this according to two views. The first: that what is meant by "the earlier generations" are the followers of the earlier Prophets before our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ).

And His saying: ﴿And a few from the later generations﴾ are from the Ummah of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The second view: that both groups are from this Ummah. This has been related in a marfu' (traced back to the Prophet) report, and it is the view of al-Hasan and Ibn Sirin. If it is said, according to the first view: how is this consistent, when the followers of the Messenger among the believers are more numerous than the followers of the Prophets? The answer: what is meant by the earlier generations is the one who saw the assembly of the Prophets and believed in them, and by the later ones is the one who saw Muhammad (ﷺ) and believed in him. It is certainly known that those [earlier ones] were among those who saw our Prophet and believed in him. For Allah, exalted is He, said concerning Yunus (peace be upon him): ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾. This refers to one Prophet alone, so how [could it be] regarding all the Prophets? Rather, this Ummah became numerous after the death of the Messenger. It has been related that "when this verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah grieved greatly because of His saying: ﴿And a few from the later generations﴾. The Prophet said: 'I truly hope that you will be a quarter of the people of Paradise, indeed a third of the people of Paradise, indeed half of the people of Paradise, and you will share with them in the second half.'" And in some reports: "The people of Paradise are one hundred and twenty rows, eighty of them from this Ummah."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 15:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿On thrones﴾. Al-surar is the plural of sarir (throne, couch). It is reported in some traditions that the height of these thrones is seventy cubits (dhira'), and it has been said that it is more than that. And Allah knows best.

His words: ﴿Woven together﴾, meaning: interlaced with rods of gold. It has also been said: interlaced and woven with pearls and rubies. In the language of the Arabs, al-wadin (the girth) is the strap with which the belly of a beast is tightened, and it was called wadin because of its weaving and the insertion of some of it into other parts. The poet said:

(You are reached by a restless [camel] whose girth is loose, / its unborn young lying across its belly, / contrary to the religion of the Christians, their religion.)

And another said:

(And of the weaving of Dawud is a woven [coat of mail] / driven along with the tribe, caravan after caravan.)

A throne that is woven (mar'mula) is lower than a throne that is not woven. It has also been said: ﴿woven together﴾ meaning: arranged in rows.

"And His saying: ﴿reclining upon them﴾. Al-ittika' (reclining) is leaning back in a manner of luxury and ease.

And His saying: ﴿upon them facing one another﴾ is like His saying: ﴿as brothers, upon couches facing one another﴾, meaning: none of them looks at the back of another, and their faces are toward the faces of their brothers."

"The saying of Allah the Exalted: ﴿There will circulate among them young boys made eternal﴾ — that is: youths.

And His saying: ﴿made eternal﴾ — that is: they do not die. It has also been said: made eternal means joyful. It has also been said: wearing earrings (muqarrat­un). The poet said:

(And women adorned with silver ornaments, as though their hindquarters were [sand-dune ridges] of the dunes)"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 18:

And His saying: ﴿with cups﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-akwab (cups) are the vessels that are round at the top and have no spouts, whereas al-abariq (ewers) are those that have spouts. In the report describing al-Kawthar, its akwab (cups) are as many as the stars of the sky.

And His saying: ﴿and a cup from a flowing spring﴾. In the tafsir it is said that the Arabs do not call a vessel a ka's (cup) unless there is wine in it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿maein﴾, that is: flowing wine. It is said: the wine of the people of Paradise is white, and it is said: red, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 19:

And His saying: ﴿They will not be affected with headache from it﴾, meaning: no headache will afflict them from drinking it, like what afflicts the drinker of wine in this world.

And His saying: ﴿nor will they be intoxicated﴾, meaning: their intellects will not be taken away. It has also been said: they will not become drunk. It has also been said: their complexions will not change. It has also been said: they will not vomit, as the drinker of wine vomits in this world. In the language, one whose color has departed is called manzuf (drained of color), and one whose intellect has departed is called nazif (intoxicated), and likewise the thirsty one. The poet said:

(So I kissed her mouth, taking hold of her temples... like the drinking of one intoxicated with the cold water of al-Hashraj)

Ibn Mas'ud recited: "wa la yunzafun" with a kasra on the zay, and its meaning: their wine will not run out.

"And fruit of what they choose" — meaning: they select.

Note on the Qur'anic quotation: ﴿وَفَاكِهَةٍ مِمَّا يَتَخَيَّرُونَ﴾ (Qur'an 56:20), rendered: "And fruit of whatever they choose."
"And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the flesh of fowl, of whatever they desire.﴾ That is, they wish for it."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 22:

And His words: ﴿And wide-eyed houris﴾ are read with the nominative (raf') in both places; it is also read with the genitive (kasr) in both places, and in the irregular (shadh) readings with the accusative (fath) in both places. On the nominative, its meaning is: "And for them are wide-eyed houris." On the genitive, its meaning is: "And they are circulated among with wide-eyed houris." On the accusative, its meaning is: "And they are given wide-eyed houris." The well-known readings are the nominative and the genitive. The houris (al-hur) were called hur because of the whiteness of their skin and the intense blackness of their eyes. It is also said: they were called hur because the gaze is bewildered (yahar) by them.

And His words: ﴿ayn﴾ mean: beautiful of eyes, and this is what we have mentioned of whiteness of complexion and blackness of the pupil.
And His saying: ﴿As if they were pearls well-guarded﴾, meaning: pearls concealed within their shells, which no hand has touched.
"And His saying: ﴿a reward for what they used to do﴾ — meaning: a recompense for them for their deeds."

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿They hear therein no idle talk nor any taking of sin﴾. That is: no false speech, and no speech for which its speaker incurs sin. Al-laghw (idle talk) is everything that is discarded as vain (yulgha).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 26:

And His saying: ﴿Except the saying "Peace, peace"﴾. Its meaning: except their saying "peace" after "peace," and greeting after greeting. It has been said that the exception here is of a different kind from what is excepted from, so it is disjunctive (munqati'), and it carries the sense of "but" (bi-ma'na lakin). It has also been said that it is of the same kind as what is excepted from, because idle talk (al-laghw) is audible speech, and hearing is audible speech. They differed over the case of His saying ﴿salaman﴾ (peace). Some of them said it is in the accusative because its meaning is: "May God grant you peace (salaman)," i.e., some of them say to one another. Others said it is in the accusative following His saying ﴿qilan﴾ (saying), because salaman is the verb mentioned.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 27:

And the Exalted One's saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand — what are the companions of the right hand!﴾ has already been explained. It is related from Maymun ibn Mihran that he said: "They have a station below the station of those brought near (al-muqarrabun)." Ja'far ibn Muhammad related from his father, from his grandfather, that they are those who mixed righteous deeds with other evil deeds and then repented.

Al-Dahhak mentioned, from Ibn 'Abbas, that God, may He be exalted, wiped the right side of Adam's back and brought forth from it offspring resembling specks (al-dharr), white; and He said to them: "Enter Paradise by My mercy." Then He wiped the left side of his back and brought forth from it offspring like black embers, and He said to them: "Enter the Fire, and I do not care." In another narration: He took with His right hand every good one, and He took with His left hand every wicked one. And in the Sahih it is (related) that "both of His hands are right." Based on this, the meaning of His saying: ﴿And the companions of the right hand﴾ is those who were taken from the right side of Adam's back.

"And His saying: ﴿In thornless lote-trees﴾, meaning: whose thorns have been cut off and removed. As-sidr (lote-tree) is the tree of the nabq (jujube-like fruit). As-Suddi said: its fruit is sweeter than honey. It was also said: makhdud means laden with fruit. And it is said: there are no pits (ajm) in its fruit. In the language, al-khadd (cutting off) means cutting. The Prophet (ﷺ), describing Makkah, said: "its trees shall not be cut" (la yakhdu shajaruha), meaning: shall not be cut down."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 29:

And His saying: ﴿And banana trees (talh) arranged in tiers﴾. ʿAlī, may Allah be pleased with him, recited it to me as "wa-ṭalʿin manḍūd" (and fruit-clusters arranged in tiers), and it is like His saying elsewhere: ﴿For it are fruit-clusters, piled high﴾. Abū Hurayrah, Abū Saʿīd al-Khudrī, Ibn ʿAbbās, al-Ḥasan and others said: it is the banana (mawz).

His saying: ﴿manḍūd﴾ means: piled one upon another. Al-Naḥḥās mentioned that the Arabs say: "ʿAsā yā fulān taṭlaḥ," meaning: may you be in blessing (niʿmah). The poet said:

(How many people have we seen perish... and we have seen a man live long in talh)

That is, in blessing. It is also said that the talh here is the tree of ʿiḍah (ʿiḍāh, thorny acacia-type trees), which is the most common tree of the Arabs, and has a fine appearance. It is narrated that when the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ went to al-Ṭāʾif, the talh there impressed them, so Allah the Exalted mentioned that they would have talh in Paradise. If someone says: how can there be a thorny tree in Paradise? We say: there is no thorn there, but it is a tree resembling talh in its size and fine appearance. It is possible that there are trees in Paradise for eating their fruit, and trees pleasing to look upon. The more correct view is that it is the banana.

And His saying, the Exalted: ﴿manḍūd﴾, they said its meaning is that its fruit and its leaves, from its base to its top, are such that it has no bare trunk (sāq bāriza).

And His saying: ﴿And extended shade﴾. Al-Hasan said: "It does not cease." And it is reported from Yahya ibn Abi Kathir that the hours of Paradise resemble the cool morning of summer. It is also said: it is like a mild, temperate air in which there is neither heat nor cold. And it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "In Paradise there is a tree in whose shade a rider could travel for a hundred years without crossing it. Recite, if you wish: ﴿And extended shade﴾."
And His saying: ﴿And water poured out﴾ — that is, poured forth (maṣbūb). Its meaning is that it is poured down upon them from above. Al-Ḥasan said: "Maskūb" means flowing, never ceasing, forever.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verses 32–33:

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And fruit in abundance, neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said: "Neither cut off" means it is not available only in one season and not in another. "Nor forbidden" means it is not withheld from anyone who wishes to reach it, as gardens are in this world. It was also said: "neither cut off" means it never ceases, and the meaning according to this is that whenever it is picked, its like or something better appears in its place immediately.

As for His words, ﴿nor forbidden﴾, it means that taking from it is not prevented. It was also said: taking from it is not prevented afterwards, nor are there thorns.

It is related from Ibn Shawdhab who said: "I saw al-Hajjaj ibn Farafisah standing in the fruit market in Basra, so I said: 'What are you doing here?' He said: 'I am looking at this cut-off, forbidden fruit.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verses 32–33:

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And fruit in abundance, neither cut off nor forbidden﴾. Al-Zajjaj (al-Zajjaj, the grammarian) said: "Neither cut off" means it is not available only in one season and not in another. "Nor forbidden" means it is not withheld from anyone who wishes to reach it, as gardens are in this world. It was also said: "neither cut off" means it never ceases, and the meaning according to this is that whenever it is picked, its like or something better appears in its place immediately.

As for His words, ﴿nor forbidden﴾, it means that taking from it is not prevented. It was also said: taking from it is not prevented afterwards, nor are there thorns.

It is related from Ibn Shawdhab who said: "I saw al-Hajjaj ibn Farafisah standing in the fruit market in Basra, so I said: 'What are you doing here?' He said: 'I am looking at this cut-off, forbidden fruit.'"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 34:

And His, may He be exalted, saying: ﴿And raised couches﴾, meaning: elevated. It is also said: some of them are above others. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Their height is the distance between the heaven and the earth, and the distance traversed between them is five hundred years." Abu 'Isa al-Tirmidhi mentioned this hadith in his book and said: it is gharib (strange, i.e. weak in its chain of transmission).

A group of the Successors (tabi'un) held that the raised couches here are the women, for the Arabs call a woman the "bed" (firash) and "covering" (libas) of a man. He named them "raised" because they are elevated in virtue, beauty and perfection, and the Arabs call every excellent person "lofty" (rafi'). It is also said: He named them "couches" because they are upon the couches, so He used the couches as a metaphor for them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 35:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We have created them with a special creation﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions: that "them" refers to the ḥūr (the maidens of Paradise), and the meaning of the creation (inshā') concerning them is that Allah, exalted is He, makes the young maidens and the old women of one age and one form in beauty and youth. And it is reported from some of the Successors (tābi'ūn) that he said regarding this verse: "They are the old women, with reddened eyelids and watery eyes." And in some narrations from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is related that he said: "A righteous woman surpasses the ḥūr in beauty by seventy times." This was mentioned by al-Naqqāsh, and it is very strange.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 36:

And His saying: ﴿So We have made them virgins﴾, meaning: maidens (ʿudhārā). Al-Ḍaḥḥāk said: The people of Paradise do not approach the women even once without finding them virgins.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 37:

And the words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿ʿUruban﴾ mean: beloved to their husbands (muhabbabat ilā azwājihinna). It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas: passionately devoted (ʿawāshiq) to their husbands. It is related from some of them: coquettish (ghunjāt). And from some of them: graceful in form (shukalāt). From some of them: ardent with desire (mughtalimāt). The Arabs say of a she-camel when she desires the stallion: ʿarūba.

And it is related from Zayd ibn Aslam: fine speech (ḥasanāt al-kalām). And from some of them: ʿuruban, meaning they speak in Arabic (al-ʿArabiyya). The first meaning is the well-known one, and it is possible to combine all these sayings, so that they are lovingly devoted to their husbands with coquetry and grace, good speech, intense affection, and in a chaste Arabic tongue.

And His saying: ﴿Atraban﴾ means: of the same age (lidāt), as though they were of one age and one birth.

It is also said: atraban means: similar to their husbands in body and stature. The poet said:

(Abrizūhā mithl al-mahāh tahādā ... bayn jins kawāʿib atrāb)

Translation:

And His words ﴿For the companions of the right﴾ mean: this which we have mentioned is for the companions of the right.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 56, verses 39–40:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿A throng from the earlier peoples, and a throng from the later peoples.﴾ That is: a company from the earlier peoples, namely those who followed the prophets and the predecessors (may the blessings of Allah be upon them all), and a company from the later peoples, namely those who followed our Prophet (ﷺ). And the thullah (throng) is a portion (qit'ah). It has been narrated by Aban ibn Abi Ayyash, from Sa'id ibn Jubayr, from Ibn 'Abbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) recited this verse: ﴿A throng from the earlier peoples, and a throng from the later peoples﴾, and said: "The two throngs are from my Ummah." Accordingly, the first throng are those who witnessed the Prophet and believed in him, and the second throng are those who believed in him without having seen him.

If it is said: How can this verse be reconciled with the preceding verse, which is His saying: ﴿And a few from the later peoples﴾? The answer: We have related that when that verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah were saddened, so Allah, the Exalted, revealed this verse. We have also mentioned the meaning of "few," which refers to those who witnessed the Prophet and followed him. Accordingly, the meaning of "throng" here is all who followed him, whether they saw him or did not see him.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 42:

His saying: ﴿In scorching wind﴾ refers to the hot wind. It is also said that it is a name of Hell (Jahannam).

And His saying: ﴿And boiling water﴾ means the water whose heat has reached its extreme. In the tafsir it is related that it issues from a rock in Hell. Also in the tafsir, on the authority of Ibn Mas'ud, it is related that the rivers of Paradise issue from a mountain of camphor in Paradise.

"And [He says]: ﴿and a shade of black smoke﴾, meaning: a black smoke that envelops the people of the Fire, and from its heat there reaches them what boils their brains. It is reported from some of them that al-Yahmum is one of the names of Jahannam (Hell). And it is reported from Ibn al-Buraydah that al-Yahmum is a mountain in the Fire; the people of the Fire are made to take shade in its shadow for a period, and then they are given permission [to come out], and from its heat there reaches them what they cry out for relief from, and this will be more severe upon them than what they were in."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 44:

And His saying: ﴿Neither cool nor pleasant.﴾ That is: neither cool of entry, nor pleasant of appearance. Al-Farra' (al-Farra') said: The Arabs make al-karim (the generous, the pleasant) a follower in every case where something is negated of it, a description intended as blame. They say: "This house is neither spacious nor pleasant (karima)," and "This horse is neither swift nor noble (karim)."

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, they were before that affluent (mutrafin).﴾ That is, they were those given comfort and luxury (mun'amin), and at-tarfah means ni'mah (blessing, comfort). In some reports: the servants of Allah are not those who indulge in luxury. And the meaning is excess (at-tawassu') in what is forbidden (al-haram) and what is not lawful; for excess in what is lawful, and enjoying comfort from it, is permissible, and one does not deserve punishment for it."

And His saying: ﴿And they used to persist in the great violation (al-hinth al-'azim)﴾. Mujahid and Qatadah said: it is shirk (polytheism). It is also said: it is the great sin. It is also said of a boy when he reaches maturity: "He has reached al-hinth," meaning: he has reached the age of sin. And from 'Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, he said: "The great hinth is the false oath (al-yamin al-fajira)." And from al-Sha'bi: it is the perjurious oath (al-yamin al-ghamus).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They used to persist﴾, meaning: they kept persisting in it until they died.

And His saying: ﴿And they used to say: "When we have died and become dust and bones, shall we indeed be raised again?"﴾ That is, the resurrection of the Day of Judgment. They said this in the manner of denial.
and His words, ﴿Or our forefathers of old?﴾ meaning: "Or will our forefathers of old be raised up after they have become dust and bones?"
The Exalted's saying: ﴿Say: Indeed, the former and the latter peoples will surely be gathered together to the appointed time of a known day﴾. It is the Day of Resurrection.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on verse 53 of Surah al-Waqi'ah (56):

And His saying: ﴿Then you will fill your bellies from it﴾. The linguists (ahl al-lughah) said: "al-shajar" (tree) is feminine and may also be treated as masculine, and ʿAli ibn ʿIsa (ʿAli ibn ʿIsa al-Rummani) mentioned it.
Its statement, "Then you will drink on it of the boiling water" (﴿فشاربون عَلَيْهِ من الْحَمِيم﴾). He said that because whoever eats something and chokes on it becomes thirsty and drinks.

And His saying: ﴿So you will drink as thirsty camels drink﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "The camels that are thirsty." According to the people of linguistic expertise (ahl al-lughah), al-Haym (a disease that afflicts camels) makes them thirst, and they are never satisfied, so they keep drinking until they die. It is also said: the drinking of al-Haym is (that of) sand, which, whenever water is poured on it, does not show any sign of it, yet it absorbs it.

This is the commentary on Qur'an 56:56, the verse "This is their hospitality (nuzul) on the Day of Judgement."

And His saying: ﴿This is their hospitality (nuzul) on the Day of Judgement﴾ — that is, their provision and their gift. If it is said: the word nuzul (hospitality, provision for a guest) is only used for honour and kindness, the answer is: when this (punishment) was placed in the position of the nuzul for the people of Paradise, He called it nuzul. This is just as He called their punishment a reward (thawab), and their threat a glad tidings (bishara). The meaning in it is what we have explained.
And His saying: ﴿We created you, so why do you not believe?﴾ That is: why do you not believe, given these evident signs? I.e., believe.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 58:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Have you considered the semen you emit?﴾ Al-imna' (emission): the casting forth of the seed (al-mani).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 59:

And His saying: ﴿Do you create it?﴾ That is: do you bring the human being into being from it (min-hu, i.e. from the seed).

And His saying: ﴿Or are We the Creators?﴾ That is: nay, rather, We are the Creators. Al-Azhari said regarding this verse: Indeed Allah, exalted is He, argued against them with the most eloquent proof for the resurrection and the bringing back to life after death in this verse. That is because the sperm (al-maniy) that falls from a human being is dead, and then Allah creates from it a living person. They acknowledged that Allah created them from drops of semen, yet they denied bringing to life after death. So He held them to account: since they acknowledged the creation of a living being from a dead drop, it follows that they must acknowledge the restoration of life to a dead thing. The meaning of the verse is: just as you have affirmed that, then affirm this.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 60:

His statement, exalted is He: ﴿We have decreed death among you﴾, means: We cause you to die, i.e., if We were unable to bring you back to life after death, We would be unable to cause you to die by taking your souls.

And His statement, exalted is He: ﴿and We are not to be outdone﴾, i.e., not to be overcome. Al-Farra' said: its meaning is: when We want to restore you, no one who outpaces Us will outpace Us, and nothing will escape Us. It is also said: if anyone other than Us wanted to do what We do, he would be unable to do it. The Arabs say: "No one outdoes me in this action (ma asbaq fi hadha al-fi'l)," i.e., no one performs an action like my action.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 61:

And His saying: ﴿Upon Our substituting your likenesses﴾, meaning: if We willed to cause you to die and create your likenesses, We would have the power to do so.

And His saying: ﴿and creating you in forms you do not know﴾, in terms of configuration and shape, meaning: if We willed, We would do that. It is said: that We would make you in the form of apes and swine. It is also said: We would create you from a place you do not know, meaning: in a world you do not know.

God's words, "And you have certainly known the first creation" (﴿وَلَقَد علمْتُم النشأة الأولى﴾), mean: the first creation, i.e., the initial act of bringing into being. He argued against them by means of the first creation for the second creation.

And His words, "Will you not then remember?" (﴿فلولا تذكرُونَ﴾), mean: will you not take admonition and reflect?

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Have you considered what you sow? Is it you who make it grow, or are We the growers?﴾ That is, "Do you cause it to sprout?" It is said of a child: "Allah sowed him (zara'ahu Allah)," meaning Allah caused him to grow.

His saying: ﴿Or are We the growers?﴾ That is, "Are We the ones who cause it to sprout?"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 65:

And His saying: ﴿Had We willed, We would have made it debris﴾, meaning: dry, crumbling and breaking into pieces, with nothing in it.

And His saying: ﴿So you would be left wondering﴾, meaning: you would be amazed. It is also said: you would regret and be grieved.

And His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are laden with debt﴾, meaning: tormented. This is what Mujahid said. Qatadah said: "Cast into misfortune." It is also reported from some of them that it derives from al-gharam (ghiram), which means destruction. It has also been said that it derives from al-ghurm (loss), because they incurred loss and gained nothing.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 67:

And His saying: ﴿Rather, we have been deprived﴾, that is: we have been deprived of good fortune, and we did not attain what we were hoping for and longing for. And it is related from Tha'lab that al-Maghram (the one afflicted with ghasm, i.e. a debt or loss) is al-Mawla' (the one who is devoted to or smitten by something). It is said: "So-and-so is maghram," meaning: mawla' with it (devoted to it). Accordingly, the meaning of His saying: ﴿Indeed, we are burdened with debt﴾ is: calamity and deprivation have afflicted us. It is also said: ﴿Indeed, we are burdened with debt﴾ means: we have been made to pay a penalty just as we were made to pay, and we have gained nothing. The poet said, using al-gharam in the sense of punishment:

(And the day of al-Nayyar and the day of al-Jafa'... they were a punishment for us, and they were a gharam [a lasting affliction])

Almost literal translation with transliterations and glosses.

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you considered﴾ [afara'aytum]. This is mentioned to draw attention to the proof contained in it.

And His saying: ﴿The water which you drink﴾ is well known."

And His saying: ﴿Is it you who sent it down from the clouds (al-muzn)?﴾ That is: from the clouds (al-sahab). Naftawayh said: al-muzn is the cloud full of water. Jarir said:

(As though it were a bright, fragrant cloud, or a pearl whose color is not hidden by its shell.)

And His saying: ﴿Or are We the ones who send it down?﴾ That is: We sent down the water from the clouds, and you did not send it down, admonishing them thereby concerning His great power.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Were We to will, We could make it bitter (ujaj).﴾ That is: intensely bitter. It has also been said: intensely salty. It is said: "al-ma' yuajju ujuja" (the water becomes ujaj) when it becomes salty. The meaning is: If We willed, We would make it ujaj, such that it could not be drunk, and by this He alerts them to gratitude.

And in some reports: the Prophet (ﷺ), when he drank, would say: "Praise be to God, who made it sweet and palatable (furat), and did not make it salty and bitter (ujaj)." Or words to this effect.

As for His saying: ﴿Then will you not be grateful?﴾ That is: will you not then be grateful?

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿Have you considered the fire that you kindle?﴾ That is: you strike (to produce fire).

It is said: "awrētu al-zand" means that one has drawn fire out of it, when the flint is struck. And it is said: "zand" and "zandah" refer to the stone from which fire is struck.

And His saying: ﴿Is it you who produced its tree?﴾, that is: did you create its tree?

And His saying: ﴿Or are We the producers?﴾, meaning: Or did We create the tree? The tree of the Fire is a well-known tree. They say: in every tree there is fire, and he has rubbed the [al-Mirkh and al-Afar].

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 73:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We have made it a reminder﴾, meaning: We have made the fire a reminder of the Greater Fire, which is the fire of Jahannam (Hell). It has been established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "Indeed, this fire of yours is one part of seventy parts of the fire of Jahannam." And in some narrations: "It was struck with water twice."

And His saying: ﴿and a provision for the wayfarers (al-muqwin)﴾. The most apparent of the opinions regarding it is that al-muqwin are the travellers, those who stop in empty, desolate lands. The second opinion is that it is for all people, both residents and travellers. According to the first opinion, the travellers are singled out, because their benefit from the fire is greater: for warmth against the cold, for light at night, and in kindling a fire there is a deterrent to beasts of prey, and the benefit of light is guidance when the way is lost.

Abu 'Ubayda said: "a provision for the wayfarers" means a benefit for everyone who has no (provisions) (zad) and no wealth.

It is said: "aqwa al-makan" when the place becomes empty of something. Al-Qutaybi and others rejected this statement, and they said: the benefit of the wealthy from the fire is greater than the benefit of the poor. The Arabs say of the poor man muqwin, and of the wealthy man muqwin: they say of the poor man muqwin because what he has is exhausted and he is empty of it, and of the wealthy man muqwin for his strength and his capacity over what the poor man cannot do. On this view, the meaning of the verse is that the fire is a benefit for all people, from the poor and the rich, the residents and the travellers.

And His saying: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾. When God mentioned the proofs against the disbelievers in the preceding verses, the point of the proof in them being that they were affirming that the one who does these things is God, and that they are incapable of them, while they deny the resurrection and the afterlife creation, God the Exalted said to them: Since you do not deny God's power over these things and the wondrous craftsmanship within them, how then do you deny His power to resurrect you and bring you back to life after your death? When He had imposed the proof upon them, He said to His Prophet, upon him be blessings and peace: ﴿So glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾, as if He were guiding him to occupy himself with declaring the Lord free of imperfection, glorifying Him and sanctifying Him, at the moment the disbelievers were left with the proof. And it is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "The best speech is 'Glory be to God and praise be to Him'" (Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi).

I swear by the setting-places of the stars.

The words of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿So I swear by the setting-places of the stars﴾. That is: "I swear" (uqsimu), and "la" (lā) is extra (ṣila), serving only for emphasis.

It has also been said that the meaning of "la" is: the matter is not as they claim, that the Qur'an is poetry, sorcery, or soothsaying; rather, "I swear by the setting-places of the stars."

It is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas that the meaning of "the setting-places of the stars" is their falling-places (masāqiṭ al-nujūm). It is also said: their setting-places and their rising-places. He swore by them because of the benefits for the servants that are connected to them.

It is also reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, in another narration, and this is the view of a large group of the Successors (tābiʿūn), among them al-Ḥasan, Qatādah, ʿIkrimah, and others, that "the setting-places of the stars" here means the stars of the Qur'an, and the meaning of "settings" (mawāqiʿ) is its descent star by star (najman najman). In a report it is stated that Allah, the Exalted, sent down the Qur'an all at once to the lowest heaven, then sent it down star by star over twenty-three years to the Prophet (ﷺ).

There is a third view regarding the verse: that what is meant by the setting-places of the stars is their scattering and falling on the Day of Resurrection.

And His saying: ﴿And indeed it is an oath, were you to know, a mighty one﴾. He said this because the oath of God is mighty, and everything by which He swears is mighty. It is also said: its being singled out as a mighty oath is because He swore by the Qur'an concerning the Qur'an; this was said by al-Qaffal al-Shashi.

The words of God, "Indeed, it is a noble Qur'an," are the place of the oath, and it is that which the oath is about [ʿalayhi].

His words, "noble" (karīm), mean abundant in good and blessing. The Arabs say: "This she-camel is karīma (noble/generous), and this date palm is karīma," when its benefits and advantages are abundant.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on Surah 56, verse 78:

His saying: ﴿In a Book well-guarded﴾ means: protected (maṣūn). It has been explained as the Preserved Tablet (al-Lawh al-Mahfūz), and it has also been explained as a Book in the heaven with the angels, in which is the Qur'an.

And His saying: ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾. Most commentators hold that it means that none touches that Book except the purified angels. Qatadah said: "As for the mushaf, everyone touches it. The intended meaning is that Book in the heaven."

The second view is that it refers to the mushaf (the written copy of the Qur'an), and that ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾ is a statement with the meaning of a prohibition, i.e., "Do not touch it except in a state of purity." It has been reported that the Prophet (ﷺ) wrote in the letter to 'Amr ibn Hazm: "And none touches the Qur'an except one who is pure."

It is also reported from 'Alqamah and al-Aswad that they entered upon Salman to have the Qur'an recited to him. He had come from the latrine, and they said to him, "Perform ablution so that we may recite the Qur'an to you." He said, "Recite to me; I do not want to touch it." Then he recited: ﴿None touches it except the purified﴾.

Qur'an 56:80 is quoted as ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾.

Translation of the commentary:

And His words: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds﴾, meaning: the Qur'an was sent down by the Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 81:

The words of the Most High: ﴿Is it this discourse that you are treating with disdain?﴾ That is: denying it with the denial of a hypocrite. The mudhin (one who is pliant or insincere) and the mudahin (one who flatters or conceals) have one meaning, and the mudahin is the one of two faces, the one whose heart is contrary to his tongue and whose tongue is contrary to his heart. It is also said: the mudhinun (mudhinun, "those who are insincere") are those who repel truth and sincerity in the best manner they are able to, and from this is the words of the Most High: ﴿They wish that you would compromise, so they would compromise﴾, meaning: you lie, so they lie, and you show off, so they show off.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 82:

And His saying: ﴿And you make your provision that you deny⁠﴾. He recited to me: "And you make your thanks that you deny," which is the meaning of the well-known reading, i.e., you place denial in the position of thanking. From this is the saying of the poet:

(Their greeting among them is a painful striking ...)

That is, they place the painful striking in the position of greeting. It is also said that the meaning of the verse is: you make the thanks for your provision that you deny, so the annexed noun (al-mudaf) was omitted and the annexed-to noun (al-mudaf ilayhi) was put in its place, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and the head has blazed with grey hair﴾, i.e., the hair of the head.

On the authority of al-Hasan al-Basri: the provision here means the guidance which Allah gave them through the Qur'an. It is as though Allah, when He sent down the Qur'an and showed them the path of truth through it, they denied it and rejected it, so that clarification was called a provision, and their denial was made ingratitude for this provision. It is also narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: "A people lost who made their share of the Qur'an denial." The third view, which is the well-known one regarding the verse, is that the provision here is the rain, and the denial is their saying: "We have been given rain by such-and-such a star." It is established by the narration of Abu Hurayrah that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Do you not see what your Lord has said? He said: 'I have not bestowed upon My servants any blessing except that a group of them becomes disbelieving in it in the morning, saying: It is the star, and by the star.'" Muslim included it in his Sahih. In another report, narrated by Mu'awiyah al-Laythi, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "A people will awake in drought, then Allah will bring them provision from Him, and they will awake as polytheists, saying: We have been given rain by such-and-such a star."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Why then, when it [the soul] reaches the throat﴾, meaning: when the soul reaches the throat. The verse is about showing their helplessness, and mentioning His power over them.
"And His saying: ﴿And you at that moment are looking on﴾ — the address is to the people of the dead person."

And His saying: ﴿But We are nearer to him than you﴾, meaning: by power. It has also been said that the Angel of Death and his assistants are meant, i.e., that they are nearer to the dying person than you are.

And His saying: ﴿but you do not see﴾, meaning: you do not see [them].

And His words, exalted is He: ﴿Then why not, if you are﴾, meaning: why not, if you are [not] under obligation, that is, not subject to command, not owned, not subdued, meaning: if you are able to do whatever you wish, and you were not in our dominion and under our power, [then] return the soul of the dead person to its place. And this is the meaning of His saying:

﴿Will you not return it, if you are truthful?﴾ This informs them of their own incapacity. It is said: "ghayr madinin" means "not held to account and not recompensed."

The first opinion is the more apt interpretation of the verse.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 88:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿As for him, if he is of those brought near﴾. In these verses Allah the Exalted mentions the condition of the three categories at death, which are the categories He mentioned at the beginning of the surah. So He said, the Exalted: ﴿As for him, if he is of those brought near﴾, that is, the foremost in good deeds, the outstanding in acts of obedience.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 89:

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Fa-rawh﴾ (then rest). The reading of ʿĀʾisha, may Allah be pleased with her, is "fa-rawh" (with a fatḥa on the rāʾ? no, with a ḍamma), and Yaʿqub al-Ḥaḍrami chose it. The more well-known reading is "farawh" with a fatḥa on the rāʾ, and its meaning is mercy (raḥma). It is also said that [rawh] means rest (istirāḥa). As for the one who reads with a ḍamma on the rāʾ, it means the everlasting life after which there is no death (fanāʾ).

In a report: "When the believer is placed in his grave and answers with the true answer, it is said to him: 'Sleep the sleep of a bride, with no worry and no distress.'" And in another report: "A door to Paradise is opened for him, and it is said to him: 'This is your place.'"

And His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿wa-rayḥān﴾ (and provision), that is, sustenance, which flows to him from Paradise in the grave. We have previously explained that rayḥān means sustenance in the poetry of the Arabs:

(Peace from God and His rayḥān... and His mercy and heaven's pearls)

Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī said: it is the rayḥān that is smelled. Abu l-Jawzāʾ said: bundles of the rayḥān of Paradise are brought, and his spirit is placed among them.

And His saying: ﴿wa-jannat naʿīm﴾ (and a Garden of bliss) is the promised Paradise. The people of tafsir said: the rawḥ and the rayḥān are in the grave, and the Garden of bliss is on the Day of Resurrection. It is also said: the rawḥ is at the time of death, the rayḥān is in the grave, and the Garden of bliss in the Resurrection at the time of being raised. It is established that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever loves meeting Allah, Allah loves meeting him; and whoever dislikes meeting Allah, Allah dislikes meeting him." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, we dislike death." He said: "No, indeed when the believer is given good news of a mercy from Allah, he loves meeting Allah, so Allah loves meeting him; and when the disbeliever is given good news of the Fire, he dislikes meeting Allah, and Allah dislikes meeting him." And he recited this verse.
"His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And as for him, if he is of the companions of the right hand﴾ — we have already explained the companions of the right hand."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 91:

And His saying: ﴿Peace be upon you from the companions of the right hand﴾, meaning: the angels will greet them with peace. It has also been said: Allah greets them with peace, and He says: "Peace be upon you" (salam 'alayka). Here "lak" means "'alayka" (upon you).

And His saying, exalted is He: ﴿from the companions of the right hand﴾, meaning: because you are of the companions of the right hand. This is the view of many of the exegetes. Some of them said: the address is to the Prophet (ﷺ), and its meaning is: "Rejoice in safety for the companions of the right hand," as if He were saying: "Do not preoccupy your heart with them, for they have attained safety." It has also been said: what is meant by the verse is that some of them greet one another with peace, as if some of them greet others with peace and congratulate them on their safety.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But if he is among the deniers, the astray, then for him is a welcome of boiling water﴾. That is, prepared for him is a drink of boiling water.
Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But if he is among the deniers, the astray, then for him is a welcome of boiling water﴾. That is, prepared for him is a drink of boiling water.
And His words ﴿and burning in Hellfire﴾ mean: entering the Hellfire. It is said: "aslāhu kadhā" meaning "he endured it" (qāsāhu). Accordingly, "taṣliyat jaḥīm" means: enduring the Hellfire.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 56, verse 95:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, this is the certain truth.﴾ That is: pure certainty, indicating that it is something that will occur without any doubt in it. It is also said that its meaning is: it is certainty of the most certain kind (aḥaqq al-yaqīn), just as one says: "ḥaqq ʿālim," meaning: a truly knowledgeable scholar.

So He says: ﴿Glorify the name of your Lord, the Mighty﴾. That is: declare your Lord free of every imperfection (tanzih) and magnify Him. It is as if He guided him to occupy himself with praising Him, glorifying Him and sanctifying Him, so that he may attain the rank of those brought near (al-muqarrabun).
